spec.description: Open an EventSub WebSocket and read every message it pushes. The first message is always `session_welcome`, carrying the session id; subscriptions created against that id with `eventsub.subscribe(...)` then deliver their events here as `notification` messages. `session_keepalive` says the connection is healthy, `session_reconnect` hands over a URL to move to, and `revocation` says a subscription has stopped and why. Nothing is ever sent to the socket: Twitch closes a connection that receives anything but a pong.

parameters.title: EventsParameters
parameters.description: The socket's own settings, sent as the connection URL's query string. The subscriptions are not here; they are created over HTTP against the session id the welcome message carries.

keepalive_timeout_seconds.description: How long Twitch may go without sending anything before it sends a `session_keepalive`, and how long the client should wait before treating the connection as lost. A whole number of seconds between 10 and 600; Twitch moves a numeric value outside that range to the nearest allowed one. Defaults to 10.

payload.title: EventSubMessage
payload.description: One message. `metadata.message_type` says which of the five kinds it is and which parts of `payload` are filled in.

metadata.title: MessageMetadata
metadata.description: Which message this is, and when Twitch sent it.

message_id.description: An ID that identifies this message, unique per session.

message_type.description: Which kind of message this is.

message_timestamp.description: When Twitch sent the message, to the nanosecond.

subscription_type.description: The subscription type this message is about, on a `notification` or a `revocation`.

subscription_version.description: The version of that subscription type, on a `notification` or a `revocation`.

payload.title: MessagePayload
payload.description: What the message carries. Empty on a `session_keepalive`, a `session` on a `session_welcome` or `session_reconnect`, a `subscription` on a `revocation`, and both a `subscription` and an `event` on a `notification`.

session.title: Session
session.description: The WebSocket session this connection carries.

id.description: The session id. This is the value an EventSub subscription names as its `transport.session_id` to deliver here.

status.description: The session's state: `connected` on a welcome, `reconnecting` on a reconnect. Left a bare string on purpose; see the notes.

keepalive_timeout_seconds.description: How long Twitch will go without sending anything before sending a keepalive. Null on a `session_reconnect`, where the setting belongs to the new connection.

reconnect_url.description: The URL to reconnect to, on a `session_reconnect`; null otherwise. Use it exactly as given: it carries its own query string. The old connection keeps delivering until the new one has been welcomed.

subscription.description: The subscription this message is about, on a `notification` or a `revocation`. On a `revocation` its `status` says why it stopped.

event.description: The event itself, on a `notification`. Its fields are a fact about `metadata.subscription_type` — a `channel.follow` event carries `user_id` and `followed_at`, a `stream.online` event carries `type` and `started_at` — so it is kept as a map. See the notes.

unverified.detail: No recording yet. Opening the socket needs no credentials, but a socket nobody has subscribed anything to only ever pushes a welcome and keepalives, and subscribing needs a user access token this machine does not hold. The Record workflow reads the socket for a bounded window through the generated client (`test/record_events.py`) and writes what arrived beside the parameters; with only the app credentials set that is the welcome and the keepalives, which is a real recording of the connect half.

notes: There is no subscribe frame to declare, so no `envelope.verb`: the connection is the subscription, the parameters travel in its URL, and Twitch closes a socket that receives anything but a pong. `push: {trigger: connect}` states that, and the mock server serves the endpoint through it. `truewire check` warns about the missing `envelope.verb` on every run; see NOTES.md.

The subscriptions this socket carries are created over HTTP, by `eventsub.subscribe(...)` naming the session id out of the welcome message. Nothing in the spec format can state that a `kind: "stream"` endpoint is fed by an `rpc` one, so it is stated here, in the README, and in NOTES.md.

The five message kinds are one `TypedDict` with `metadata.message_type` as the discriminator, not five variants in an `anyOf`. A caller narrows on `message["metadata"]["message_type"]`, which is a `Literal` of the five values; see NOTES.md for why the union form is worse here.

The `event` object is a map: its fields depend on the subscription type, of which Twitch documents dozens, and declaring a handful of them would type the others wrong. `metadata.subscription_type` is what says how to read it.
`session.status` is left a bare string: the reference shows `connected` and `reconnecting` in its examples but publishes no closed list of session states.

Written from the Helix reference at the `docs` URL above. Fields the reference marks deprecated are not declared; an undeclared field passes validation and is dropped from the validated value, so a recording that carries one is still valid. The first recording confirms or corrects the rest.
